extracted.intended_audience: marine and civil engineers, shipwrights, government officials and researchers concerned with marine timber preservation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of methods to protect timber (piles, sluice-gates, marine works) from the marine borers Teredo navalis and related organisms, based on multi-year controlled experiments and field observations. Includes grouping of methods, specific treatments tested, experimental protocol, and practical conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coatings applied to the surface of wood
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface coatings or modifications of the wood surface were tested as a group of methods intended to prevent young teredo from attaching or penetrating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods examined include: Claasen's secret method and metallic paint; Brinkerink's hot mixture of Russian talc, coal-tar, resin, sulphur and powdered glass applied ~2 mm thick; Rijswijk's analogous method; paraffine varnish from peat distillation; coal-tar applied cold or hot (including tar-filled bored holes); paints mixed with turpentine/linseed-oil (chrome-green, verdigris); singeing/superficial carbonization. Experimental outcome: none of these surface applications afforded lasting protection. Partial early exceptions (e.g., some coal-tar treatments) failed on longer exposure. Reasoning: surface coverings are liable to be injured or dissolved by water, ice, or mechanical action; any small uncovered point allows microscopic teredos to penetrate. Practical note: covering with iron nails or metal sheets protects only while the covering remains unbroken and is costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metallic armoring (nails, copper/zinc sheets) as protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of nails (a 'coat-of-mail') or sheets of iron/copper/zinc to physically shield wood from teredo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although such coverings prevent teredo while intact, they are expensive and only protective so long as the surface remains unbroken. For nails, square heads must join exactly and controlled rusting is sometimes used to close interstices; nevertheless, piles with thick rust incrustation have been found eaten internally. Sheets of metal on sluice-gates are effective only until broken by water or ice. Thus metallic armoring is not an infallible long-term solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impregnation of wood with inorganic soluble salts
rubrics_metrics.description: Impregnating timber with inorganic soluble salts (often presumed poisonous to fish/animals) as a method of preserving wood from teredo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific salts tested include sulphate of copper, sulphate of protoxide of iron (green vitriol), acetate of lead, and combined treatments (soluble glass then chloride of calcium). Experimental outcome: these impregnations did not protect wood from teredo. Reasons given: salts are leached out by sea-water and/or do not have a poisonous effect on teredo. Historical trials with mercurial and arsenical salts and corrosive sublimate had also been found ineffective elsewhere, so the commission omitted repeating some tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oil of paraffine (peat-derived) impregnation
rubrics_metrics.description: Impregnation of timber with oil of paraffine produced by dry distillation of peat, tested as a preservative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial results: after one summer some paraffine-treated pieces resisted teredo. Experimental protocol: sets of ten pieces were placed and one withdrawn yearly for inspection. Later findings: after additional years (by November 1863) fully developed teredos were found even in previously resistant pieces (both oak and red fir) when surfaces were removed for inspection. Conclusion: paraffine provided only temporary resistance and did not ensure long-term protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oil of creosote (creosoted wood) as the primary preservative
rubrics_metrics.description: Impregnation of timber with creosote oil (product of dry distillation of coal-tar) as a preservative against teredo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive multi-year experiments showed creosoted wood resisted teredo attacks far better than untreated wood across multiple ports and wood types. Key caveats: creosote must be of good quality, impregnation must be thorough, and woods used should readily absorb oil (resinous woods and southern yellow pine absorb well; oak is more difficult). Practices to achieve thorough impregnation include withdrawing sap in vacuum and treating with hot oils under heavy pressure for fir. Evidence: properly creosoted pine and fir remained entirely intact after several summers; insufficiently penetrated areas showed teredo galleries. Creosote's insolubility in water contributes to its efficacy. Petroleum was considered but rejected on economic grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and completeness of impregnation as a determinant of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of penetration of the preservative into the wood (not merely surface coverage) determines whether wood is truly protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commission's protocol removed a few millimetres of surface from test pieces each year to reveal galleries; this distinguishes superficial surface protection from true impregnation. Observed failures (e.g., in oak creosoted poorly at Amsterdam) occurred at points where the oil had not penetrated. Junctions with unprepared wood permitted teredo to reach creosoted wood. Practical implication: thorough impregnation and use of species that absorb oil readily are essential for long-term success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exotic/hard woods is not a reliable protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing whether exotic or very hard woods resist teredo attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments and observations showed that hardness is not an obstacle: specimens of guaiacum, mamberklak, American oaks, and others have been found completely eaten. Thus reliance on hard exotic woods alone is not a guaranteed preservative strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological coverage (barnacles, mussels) can be protective if established first
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural encrusting by cirripeds (barnacles) or mussels can prevent young teredo from attaching and penetrating wood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When barnacles or other shellfish cover the wood surface so densely that disks touch and leave no vacant surface, young teredo cannot attach. This preservative effect holds even when shells fall if disks remain adhered. Lehmann proposed deliberately planting common mussels (Mytilus edulis) to exploit this effect. Condition: the covering must be present before teredo settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and practical constraints on chosen remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of methods should account for practical cost and long-term durability under marine conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: metallic armoring (nails, metal sheets) is very costly; petroleum, even if effective, is impractical due to high price; surface coatings are vulnerable to damage. The commission weighed efficacy against expense and durability when recommending methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design and controls for testing wood-preservation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of a rigorous experimental protocol to assess efficacy of preservation methods against teredo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commission's best practices included: using pieces of the same kinds of wood placed side-by-side with untreated counter-proofs; having the inventors prepare samples when possible to avoid unfairness; using ten replicates per treatment and withdrawing one piece annually for up to ten years for examination; placing samples in multiple ports/localities; fastening treated and untreated pieces together to detect cross-contamination; removing outer shavings (a few millimetres) to detect internal galleries; replacing intact pieces to continue exposure. These controls ensured reliable, impartial, long-term evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment criterion: detect internal galleries by removing surface layers
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to determine whether apparent protection is only superficial or indicates true impregnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In examination, the commission removed the outside of the wood to a depth of some millimetres with an adze to reveal galleries of teredos if present. Pieces found intact after this removal were replaced in the water and re-tested in subsequent years. This method isolates superficial surface effects from impregnation-based preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and historical factors affecting teredo outbreaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding and considering environmental conditions that favor teredo proliferation when evaluating preservation needs and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commission and earlier observers linked prodigious teredo increases to combinations of moderate rainfall, falling river levels, increased salinity of estuarine/arm waters, and elevated temperature. Historical/fossil evidence shows teredo has long been present. Such environmental context affects the urgency and expected performance of protective measures.
